concepts.name: OPEC: Founding, Structure and Membership Criteria
key_dimensions: Founded in 1960 at Baghdad Conference — founding members: Iran, Iraq, Kuwait, Saudi Arabia, Venezuela (trap: NOT UAE or Libya at founding)
Headquarters: Vienna, Austria (trap: often confused with IEA headquarters also in Vienna)
Membership criteria: substantial net exports of crude oil + sharing interests of member countries — no formal GDP or reserve threshold
Difference between full members, associate members, and observer status — OPEC has no formal 'observer' category unlike WTO

concepts.name: OPEC's Core Mandate and Production Quota Mechanism
key_dimensions: Primary objective: coordinate petroleum policies to secure fair/stable prices for producers and efficient supply to consumers
Production quotas allocated per member — basis: proven reserves, historical production, economic needs (no single universal formula)
Unanimous vs. majority voting — major decisions require consensus, creating frequent deadlock scenarios
Distinction between OPEC's stated mandate (price stability) vs. critics' view (cartel behaviour and supply manipulation)

concepts.name: OPEC+ Formation: Expansion Beyond Original OPEC
key_dimensions: OPEC+ formed in 2016 after oil price crash — includes 10 non-OPEC oil producers led by Russia
Key non-OPEC members in OPEC+: Russia, Mexico, Kazakhstan, Azerbaijan (trap: Mexico rejoined but has complex participation history)
OPEC+ is NOT a formal treaty-based organisation — it is a voluntary coalition/alliance, unlike original OPEC which has a statute
Implications of OPEC+ for global oil price governance vs. OPEC-only decisions — OPEC+ controls ~40% of global oil supply

concepts.name: Saudi Arabia's Dominant Role and 'Swing Producer' Concept
key_dimensions: Saudi Arabia holds ~17% of global proven reserves — largest within OPEC, giving de facto veto power
Swing producer: ability to rapidly increase/decrease output to stabilise prices — Saudi Arabia is the classic example
Saudi Aramco's role: state-owned, largest oil company by revenue — distinguishing company policy from state policy
2014 Saudi strategy of NOT cutting output (market share war vs. US shale) — departure from traditional swing producer role

concepts.name: OPEC and the 1973 Oil Embargo: Geopolitical Weaponisation of Oil
key_dimensions: Arab members of OPEC (OAPEC — different from OPEC, trap!) imposed embargo against US, Netherlands for supporting Israel in Yom Kippur War
OAPEC vs. OPEC distinction: OAPEC is Arab-specific, OPEC is broader — Iran and Venezuela are in OPEC but NOT OAPEC
Consequences: oil prices quadrupled, stagflation in West, birth of IEA (1974) as a counter-institution
Lesson for UPSC: resource nationalism, energy security as strategic tool, India's vulnerability as oil importer

concepts.name: International Energy Agency (IEA) vs. OPEC: Institutional Rivalry
key_dimensions: IEA created in 1974 as OECD response to OPEC embargo — headquartered in Paris (trap: both IEA and OPEC are in Europe but different cities)
IEA mandate: energy security for consumer nations, strategic petroleum reserves (SPR) coordination
IEA membership restricted to OECD countries historically — India became Associate member in 2017, full accession ongoing
OPEC vs. IEA as producer-consumer axis of global energy governance — recent cooperation on climate/clean energy adds complexity

concepts.name: OPEC's Evolving Membership: Entries, Exits and Suspensions
key_dimensions: Ecuador: joined 1973, suspended 1992, rejoined 2007, exited again 2020 — longest re-joining history (trap question on current membership)
Qatar exited OPEC in 2019 to focus on LNG (not oil) — first Gulf state to exit; signals diversification away from crude
Indonesia: rejoined 2016, suspended again same year — net oil importer status made quota compliance impossible
Gabon, Congo, Equatorial Guinea as newer African members — highlights OPEC's geographic diversification beyond Middle East

concepts.name: Russia–OPEC Relationship and the 2020 Oil Price War
key_dimensions: March 2020: Russia refused Saudi demand to cut production → Saudi Arabia flooded market → oil prices crashed to historic lows (WTI briefly negative)
COVID-19 demand collapse compounded the supply glut — dual shock scenario unique in OPEC history
Resolution: OPEC+ agreed to largest-ever production cut (9.7 million bpd) in April 2020
Structural tension: Russia's fiscal breakeven price vs. Saudi breakeven — determines floor of cooperation

concepts.name: OPEC's Oil Revenue Recycling ('Petrodollar') System
key_dimensions: Petrodollar: oil sold globally in USD → OPEC nations accumulate USD → reinvested in US Treasuries/Western assets
Origin: 1974 US-Saudi agreement linking oil pricing to USD — underpins dollar's reserve currency status
Recent challenge: China negotiating yuan-denominated oil contracts with Saudi Arabia — 'petroyuan' threat to dollar hegemony
India's angle: India–UAE local currency oil trade, rupee-dirham settlements — strategic implication for UPSC current affairs

concepts.name: OPEC Fund for International Development (OFID)
key_dimensions: Established 1976, headquartered in Vienna — OPEC's development finance arm (trap: different from OPEC itself)
Mandate: provide concessional loans to non-OPEC developing countries — explicitly includes non-oil developing nations
Rebranded as 'the OPEC Fund' in 2021 — UPSC may test new vs. old name
Comparison with other multilateral development banks: OFID is sector-agnostic (energy, agriculture, health) unlike name suggests

concepts.name: US Shale Revolution and Its Impact on OPEC's Market Power
key_dimensions: Hydraulic fracturing (fracking) made US world's largest oil producer by 2018 — eroded OPEC's ability to single-handedly control prices
OPEC's market share fell from ~55% (1970s) to ~40% (2020s) — structural decline in pricing power
Break-even price of US shale (~$40–55/barrel) acts as a natural price ceiling for OPEC cuts strategy
OPEC+ formation partly a response to shale — need for larger coalition to counterbalance US production

concepts.name: OPEC and Climate Change: Energy Transition Dilemma
key_dimensions: OPEC nations hold majority of 'stranded asset' risk under aggressive decarbonisation scenarios
Saudi Vision 2030, UAE Net Zero 2050 — OPEC members' domestic diversification strategies vs. collective oil dependence
OPEC's position in UNFCCC negotiations: historically resistant to binding emission cuts, lobbying against 'phase out' language (COP28 in UAE)
Tension: IEA's 2021 report said no new oil/gas fields needed under Net Zero 2050 — directly contradicts OPEC investment plans

concepts.name: Strategic Petroleum Reserves (SPR) as Counter to OPEC Pricing Power
key_dimensions: IEA members mandated to hold 90 days of net oil imports as SPR — emergency release mechanism
US SPR: largest strategic reserve globally (~700 million barrels), released multiple times including 2022 post-Ukraine war
India's SPR: ~5 million tonnes in underground caverns at Visakhapatnam, Mangalore, Padur — managed by ISPRL
SPR release logic: counteract supply shocks from OPEC cuts or geopolitical disruptions — limits OPEC's pricing leverage

concepts.name: India–OPEC Energy Relationship and Diversification Strategy
key_dimensions: India is world's 3rd largest oil importer (~85% import dependent) — OPEC supplies ~60–70% of India's oil imports
India's strategy: diversify away from Middle East OPEC — increased imports from US, Russia, Brazil
Post-2022 Russia sanctions: India dramatically increased Russian crude imports (discounted Urals crude) — reducing OPEC share
India's 'buyer's leverage' argument: as major consumer, India pushes back on OPEC production cuts affecting developing economies

concepts.name: Venezuela and Iran: Sanctioned OPEC Members and Quota Complications
key_dimensions: Venezuela: holds world's largest proven oil reserves (~304 billion barrels) but production collapsed due to economic crisis and US sanctions
Iran: under US JCPOA-related sanctions — exempt from OPEC production quotas as it cannot produce at full capacity
Exemption mechanism: OPEC grants exemptions to sanctioned/conflict-affected members (Libya, Iran, Venezuela) — trap: these exemptions distort headline quota numbers
Geopolitical angle: lifting of Iran sanctions could add 1–2 million bpd to market — significant price impact scenario

concepts.name: OPEC's Relationship with Natural Gas and LNG Markets
key_dimensions: OPEC's mandate is specifically crude oil — natural gas is NOT covered under OPEC framework
Gas Exporting Countries Forum (GECF): the 'gas OPEC' — headquartered in Doha, Qatar; includes Russia, Iran, Qatar
Qatar's 2019 exit from OPEC explicitly to focus on LNG — highlights oil vs. gas strategic divergence
Trap: GECF does NOT have production quotas like OPEC — it is more of a consultative forum, not a cartel

concepts.name: OPEC's Pricing Benchmarks: Brent, WTI and OPEC Basket
key_dimensions: OPEC Reference Basket (ORB): weighted average of prices of petroleum blends from member countries — different from Brent/WTI
Brent Crude (North Sea) = global benchmark for ~2/3 of world's oil contracts; WTI (West Texas) = US benchmark
OPEC sets production targets, NOT prices directly — prices emerge from market based on supply-demand, with ORB as indicator
Trap: OPEC does NOT directly 'fix' oil prices — it influences them through supply management; price-fixing would violate WTO/antitrust norms for member states

concepts.name: Africa's Growing Role in OPEC and 'New OPEC' Discourse
key_dimensions: Current African OPEC members: Nigeria, Libya, Algeria, Gabon, Congo, Equatorial Guinea — Nigeria is Africa's largest producer
Non-OPEC African producers: Angola (exited OPEC 2023 citing quota disputes), South Africa, Ghana, Senegal emerging
Angola's 2023 exit: dissatisfied with production quota allocation — signals centrifugal pressures within OPEC
'New OPEC' discourse: possibility of African oil producers forming regional bloc — currently not materialised but relevant for geopolitics questions

concepts.name: Cartel Theory and OPEC's Legal Status Under International Law
key_dimensions: OPEC technically functions as a cartel (coordinated supply restriction) but enjoys sovereign immunity — member states, not companies, set policy
NOPEC Bill (US Congress): proposed legislation to allow US to sue OPEC nations under antitrust law — never passed, but signals political pressure
Distinction: private cartels (illegal under competition law) vs. sovereign state coordination (protected by international law principles)
WTO interface: WTO rules generally do not apply to natural resource export restrictions by sovereign states — key legal gap OPEC exploits

concepts.name: OPEC's Institutional Decision-Making: Conference, Board of Governors, Secretariat
key_dimensions: OPEC Conference: supreme authority — meets twice yearly (June and December), each member has one vote, decisions by unanimous agreement
Board of Governors: manages affairs between Conferences — each member nominates one governor
Secretary-General: administrative head — current (2023): Haitham Al Ghais of Kuwait (trap: not Saudi — Secretaries-General rotate among members)
Differentiation from other bodies: OPEC has no dispute resolution mechanism unlike WTO, and no enforcement power over member quotas — 'cheating' is endemic
